doc.title: Joe Wilder Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 12, 1998

title: Classical ambitions and the Del Staigers record prank on Dick Perry
summary: Wilder always practiced classical music and admired cornetist Del Staigers; he tells how he tricked 'Lorelei' trumpeter Dick Perry with a smashed record.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: Were you aspiring to play in a classical situation at that time also?

Well yes I did, and even while I was with the band I always practiced a lot of classical things, not thinking that I would ever get an opportunity to play in a symphony orchestra, but I just did it because of my interest in that. And when I was younger I heard Del Staigers , who, he’s one, and I’m sure I heard Herbert Clarke and Walter Smith, people like that who were very famous cornet soloists. But I remember Del Staigers for some reason or other better than the others, and I always wanted to play like Del Staigers . He could double tongue and triple tongue and all this. And apropos of that, Dick Perry, who was the first trumpet player with “Lorelei,” he was playing first trumpet, that’s how it was, and he knew, I had mentioned several times that I liked Del Staigers . So one day he says “you know I have two recordings of Del Staigers.” And he said “they’re in a double album thing.” And he said “one day I’ll bring it in and you can take it home and you can put it on a cassette and record it, and then bring them back to me.” So I said “okay.” And © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -9-

he did that. He brought them in. So I took it home and it was Del Staigers , and he had a very high pitched voice “and now when you do this —” you do so and so and so and so. He had a voice like that. But his playing was really beautiful. And of course the recording wasn’t that great because of the time at which it was done. So I thought to myself, now what can I do to put Dick Perry on when I go back with these recordings? And I had one of these big LP’s on rubber about that thick, those old recordings, it was of no use. And I took this thing and threw it on the floor, and it ended up in about 50 small pieces you know, and I put these in this envelope with his recording, the two recordings. So when I came into the theater I was coming and I saw him and some of the other guys and I nudged one of the other fellows coming in and I said, “watch this.” And I pretended I stumbled on the stairs, and as I did I turned this envelope and these pieces are falling out of the envelope on the floor. And I said, “oh my God, Dick, I’m so sorry,” I said, “I just dropped the records,” and I said, “look at this.” And Pete said he’s sitting there and he’s almost like almost pale. Finally he said, “well, you did put it on cassette didn’t you?” I said, “yeah I did record it.” And then I started laughing, I started smiling. He looked at me and he said “you know what?” He said, “I know what it is, you’re up to one of your dirty tricks.” I just broke up. I mean if you could have seen the expression on his face when this manila envelope turned out these pieces falling all over.
